extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer review researchers, and academic staff responsible for reviewer recruitment/training
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and measurable criteria used by an academic medical journal to select reviewers, score individual peer reviews, and evaluate reviewer performance (including interventions to improve review quality). Focuses on editor-assigned ratings, temporal trends, reviewer selection, mentoring, and training metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor-assigned review quality rating (1–5 scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: All reviews are routinely rated by editors on a previously reported 5-point scale. The score is recorded contemporaneously within the journal's editorial management software and was used as the primary outcome measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale anchors: 3 = 'acceptable', 4 = 'good', 5 = 'exceptional, hard to improve'. The scale has demonstrated moderate reliability and is comparable to the van Rooyen Review Quality Instrument (RQI). Used to compute mean review quality scores for reviewers and cohorts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of the review to the editor and authors (gold standard; 6 essential components)
rubrics_metrics.description: The gold standard for the editor quality score is the usefulness of the review to the editor (and authors), consisting of 6 essential specific components (described in detail elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the six components are defined in other work, they underpin the editor's 1–5 quality rating and are the conceptual basis for judging a review's overall usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slope of change in reviewer quality over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Change (improvement or deterioration) in editor-assigned reviewer quality ratings from the first review until the study end date, expressed as the slope of quality score trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzed using linear mixed effects models that control for within-reviewer and between-reviewer trends, as well as between-editor and within-editor trends. Used as a primary measure of whether training/mentoring produces longitudinal improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection: prior publication requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be approved as a new reviewer the candidate must have already published at least two first-author peer-reviewed publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural selection criterion is used by the journal before adding someone to the reviewer pool and thus functions as an eligibility/quality filter on incoming reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentor selection: top reviewer (top 50) status
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentors were senior reviewers who volunteered and had to have made the 'top 50' reviewer list for at least two of the past four years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'top 50' list ranks reviewers by a formula including timeliness, quality scores, and review volume; mentors therefore represent an elite group (about top 5% of reviewers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeliness of reviewers (promptness in returning reviews) is a component of reviewer quality and is part of the formula used to rank top reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness is operationalized in editorial systems (e.g., percent of invitations declined, mean time to complete), and contributes to selection for mentor roles and stratification systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review volume / productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of reviews performed/completed by a reviewer (used both as a performance metric and as a component of mentor ranking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported as mean number of reviews completed, invitations received, and invitations declined; used in calculations for reviewer ranking and to describe engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of manuscript errors / critical appraisal ability
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability of a reviewer to detect errors in manuscripts and perform critical appraisal of methodology and generalizability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior training interventions sometimes improved error identification marginally but effects often waned. Training in critical appraisal is a target outcome for reviewer improvement efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crafting accurate feedback to authors (helpfulness/actionability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good review should inform editors about study strengths and weaknesses and craft accurate, constructive feedback to authors about how to improve their manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functional criterion of usefulness underlies editor ratings and is what mentoring/training aims to improve (mentors were asked to comment on how well mentees addressed these elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision and use of peer review learning resources (editor feedback, other reviewers' comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal practice of providing reviewers, after decisions are made, with blinded copies of other reviewers' comments and the editor's decision letter as a potential learning tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers rated how useful such features were to their peer review experience; access to peer reviewers' comments and editor feedback is considered part of standard mentoring/training resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal training exposure (courses, workshops, online modules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior formal training in peer review, formal training in critical appraisal, and structured workshops are measured as prior experiences and potential contributors to review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveyed reviewers rated perceived usefulness of such experiences. The journal also encourages completion of an online peer review training module (not enforced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer satisfaction and perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentee satisfaction and perspectives on mentoring and training programs, collected via post-intervention survey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary outcome: asked how many contacts with mentor, communication medium (email/phone), and subjective opinions regarding usefulness of the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability of editors' subjective quality ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors' subjective ratings of review quality have demonstrated moderate reliability in prior work and are used as operational quality measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although subjective, these ratings have been validated and compared favorably to instruments like the RQI; journals rely on them for quality monitoring and research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of validated instruments (Review Quality Instrument, RQI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to van Rooyen's Review Quality Instrument (RQI) as a validated tool for assessing peer review quality; the journal's 1–5 scale is comparable to the RQI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RQI or similar validated instruments can be used to operationalize components of a 'good review' and to standardize measurement across studies and journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer stratification by quality and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation of a reviewer stratification system that ranks and classifies reviewers based on measured quality and reliability metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stratification systems use metrics like quality scores, timeliness, and volume to identify high-performing reviewers and to inform selection/assignment policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures of reviewer engagement (invitations accepted/declined)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational engagement metrics such as number of invitations to review, number/percent declined, and mean number of reviews completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to describe reviewer behavior and availability; also can affect assignment patterns, mentor pairing, and interpretation of quality metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentor feedback content and process
rubrics_metrics.description: In the intervention mentors were asked to comment on how well the mentee addressed key elements of a good review, what they might have done differently, and to rate their own review on the journal's 1–5 scale; the amount and content of communication were left flexible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentor feedback was neither standardized nor observed; the study notes that lack of standardized, prompt, and intensive feedback may limit effectiveness of mentoring interventions.
